12 Two parts of a sailing boat are the mast and the boom. The mast is a vertical rigid beam and the
boom is a horizontal rigid beam. One end of the boom is attached to the mast by a pivot. The
other end of the boom is connected to the mast by a rope, as shown.
rope
T
mast

pivot
200 N
boom
The rope is at an angle of 40 to the horizontal and exerts a tension force T on the boom. The
weight of the boom is 200 N. The mass of the boom is uniformly distributed along its length. The
boom is in equilibrium.
What is the magnitude of T ?
A
130 N
B
160 N
C
260 N
D
310 N

hints: Notice the pivot at the mast end of the boom - taking moments about the pivot removes the unknown pivot force from the equation.
The uniform $200 \text{ N}$ boom acts at its centre, so its clockwise moment arm is half the boom length while tension $T$ acts at the full length.
Only the vertical part of the rope tension, $T \sin 40^{\circ}$, is perpendicular to the horizontal boom and provides the anticlockwise moment.
walkthrough: Take moments about the pivot so the unknown contact force at the pivot has zero moment and can be ignored.
The boom is uniform, so the $200 \text{ N}$ weight acts at the midpoint. If boom length is $L$, its clockwise moment is $200 \times L/2 = 100L$.
The rope pulls at $40^{\circ}$ to the horizontal at distance $L$ from the pivot. The perpendicular component is $T \sin 40^{\circ}$ upward.
Its anticlockwise moment about the pivot is $T \sin 40^{\circ} \times L$.
For equilibrium, sum of moments is zero: $T \sin 40^{\circ} \times L = 100L$.
Cancel $L$ and solve: $T = 100/\sin 40^{\circ} \approx 100/0.643 \approx 156 \text{ N}$, about $160 \text{ N}$. This is option B.

A.explanation: About $130 \text{ N}$ comes from using the full $200 \text{ N}$ at the centre with an incorrect moment arm or trig factor, not $T \sin 40^{\circ}$ balancing half the weight.

B.explanation: Taking moments about the pivot gives $T \sin 40^{\circ} = 100 \text{ N}$, so $T \approx 156 \text{ N}$, close to $160 \text{ N}$.

C.explanation: About $260 \text{ N}$ treats the $200 \text{ N}$ weight as acting at the end of the boom instead of at its centre at half the length.

D.explanation: About $310 \text{ N}$ uses $T \cos 40^{\circ}$ for the vertical component and puts the weight at the end, giving $T = 200/\cos 40^{\circ}$.
